scope: Original core flashcards already selected by real first-mock filter: Physics AS, taught Chemistry AS+A2, Maths Year 1 Pure; 15 carefully selected one-skill cards per subject.
checks: Two correct synonyms and two common incorrect misconceptions per existing card; original ID, front, back and previous accepted/rejected answers must be preserved; acceptance/rejection checked against production evaluator before merge.

records.subject: Physics
records.front: When is diffraction most noticeable?
records.back: When the gap size is comparable with the wavelength.
accept: strongest spreading occurs when gap width is about a wavelength
aperture comparable in size to lambda
reject: diffraction is greatest when the gap is much larger than the wavelength
diffraction requires a wave to be absorbed

records.subject: Physics
records.front: Define emf.
records.back: Energy supplied by the source per unit charge.
accept: work done by the power source per unit charge
the source's supplied energy divided by charge
reject: emf is the energy transferred per second
emf equals resistance multiplied by time

records.subject: Physics
records.front: State Newton's first law precisely, including the condition on resultant force.
records.back: If resultant external force is zero, an object stays at rest or moves at constant velocity in a straight line.
accept: with zero net external force an object stays at rest or travels at constant velocity
zero resultant force implies no change in velocity
reject: zero resultant force means the object must come to rest
constant velocity always requires a nonzero resultant force

records.subject: Physics
records.front: State Newton's second law in its general momentum form.
records.back: Resultant external force equals the rate of change of momentum, in the force direction: F = Δp/Δt (or dp/dt).
accept: net external force is dp/dt
the rate of momentum change equals the resultant force
reject: net force equals momentum divided by displacement
F equals momentum multiplied by time

records.subject: Physics
records.front: A heavy lorry hits a small car. Which experiences the greater force during their interaction?
records.back: Neither: by Newton's third law their interaction forces have equal magnitude, opposite direction; accelerations can differ.
accept: the truck and car exert equal and opposite forces on each other
their interaction forces are the same magnitude by Newton's third law
reject: the heavier lorry exerts a bigger force
the lighter car exerts a bigger force because its acceleration is greater

records.subject: Physics
records.front: Why does the normal reaction on a simple slope not equal the full weight?
records.back: The surface balances only the perpendicular component, mg cosθ; weight mg is vertical.
accept: only the perpendicular component of weight, mg cos theta, is supported by the plane
on a simple incline the normal reaction balances mg cos theta
reject: the normal reaction must equal mg on any incline
the normal reaction always equals mg sin theta

records.subject: Physics
records.front: On a slope, why resolve weight parallel and perpendicular to the surface?
records.back: Normal acceleration is zero; along the slope there may be a resultant force and acceleration.
accept: perpendicular components balance but along-slope resultant can accelerate the body
resolving separates the normal balance and possible parallel acceleration
reject: all the weight acts only along the slope
there is always a nonzero acceleration perpendicular to a fixed slope

records.subject: Physics
records.front: Why can't you double ascent time to find flight time when a projectile lands below launch height?
records.back: The vertical journey is asymmetric; use vertical displacement and solve a quadratic for landing time.
accept: the descent is not symmetric about maximum height when final height differs
the landing level is lower so use vertical displacement and solve for the total time
reject: flight time always equals twice the time to the maximum height
horizontal motion determines the flight time without vertical displacement

records.subject: Physics
records.front: What happens to a projectile's horizontal velocity at its highest point?
records.back: It is unchanged without air resistance; only vertical velocity is zero at the top.
accept: the horizontal velocity is constant if air resistance is ignored
at the top vx is unchanged whereas vy is zero
reject: the projectile's horizontal velocity becomes zero at its peak
gravity makes the horizontal velocity increase with time when drag is absent

records.subject: Physics
records.front: Given velocity components vₓ and vᵧ just before impact, how do you find impact speed?
records.back: Impact speed is √(vₓ² + vᵧ²), not merely the magnitude of the vertical velocity.
accept: use Pythagoras on velocity components: sqrt(vx^2+vy^2)
speed equals the magnitude of the vector with components vx and vy
reject: impact speed is always just the vertical component
impact speed is vx plus vy even when perpendicular

records.subject: Physics
records.front: If v<0 and a<0, what happens to speed?
records.back: Speed increases because velocity and acceleration point in the same negative direction.
accept: the object speeds up when v and a are both negative
acceleration in the direction of negative velocity increases the magnitude of v
reject: a negative acceleration always reduces speed
negative velocity always means the object is slowing down

records.subject: Physics
records.front: What does area under a force–time graph represent?
records.back: Impulse, equal to change in momentum.
accept: integrating force with respect to time gives change in momentum
the area represents impulse in newton seconds
reject: force-time graph area is mechanical work in joules
force-time area gives acceleration directly

records.subject: Physics
records.front: Displacement–time: what does a negative gradient mean?
records.back: Velocity is negative: motion in the negative direction, not necessarily slowing down.
accept: a negative displacement-time slope means velocity is negative
it moves in the negative direction and may speed up or slow down
reject: negative displacement-time gradient proves the object is decelerating
a negative gradient means positive velocity

records.subject: Physics
records.front: Why is total distance different from displacement on a v–t graph?
records.back: Distance sums all absolute areas; displacement uses signed areas.
accept: add absolute areas for distance but algebraic signed areas for displacement
total distance counts both positive and negative velocity regions as positive
reject: distance equals positive area minus the magnitude of negative area
signed area always gives total distance travelled

records.subject: Physics
records.front: Acceleration–time area gives which quantity?
records.back: Change in velocity, not displacement or distance.
accept: the signed integral of acceleration over time is delta v
the area of a against time gives the velocity change
reject: area under acceleration-time is displacement
acceleration-time area directly gives total distance

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: What does an acyl chloride form with an alcohol?
records.back: An ester and HCl.
accept: acyl chloride and alcohol produce an ester plus hydrogen chloride
an ester forms and HCl is released
reject: an acyl chloride and alcohol produce an amide
the main products are an aldehyde and hydrogen

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: What happens when an acyl chloride reacts with water?
records.back: A carboxylic acid and HCl are formed.
accept: water hydrolyses an acyl chloride to the carboxylic acid and HCl
hydrolysis yields RCOOH and hydrogen chloride
reject: hydrolysis produces a primary amide
acyl chloride and water produce an alcohol and chlorine gas

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: What is the general formula of an acyl chloride?
records.back: R–C(=O)–Cl.
accept: RCOCl
R-C(=O)-Cl
reject: RCOOH
RCOOR

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: What is an acyl group?
records.back: R–C(=O)–, the group transferred in acylation.
accept: RCO- is the acyl group
R-C(=O)-, transferred in acylation
reject: R-OH is the acyl group
the acyl group is -NH2

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: What group links the two carbonyls in an acid anhydride?
records.back: A bridging oxygen: RCO–O–COR′.
accept: one oxygen links the two acyl groups
anhydride linkage is -C(=O)-O-C(=O)-
reject: a nitrogen connects the two carbonyl groups
the carbonyl carbons bond directly without oxygen

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: What is an amide functional group?
records.back: A carbonyl directly bonded to nitrogen, e.g. –CONH₂.
accept: an amide contains -C(=O)-N-
the functional group has a nitrogen attached directly to a carbonyl carbon
reject: an amide contains only C-N single bonds without a carbonyl
the amide functional group is -COO-

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: How does an amide differ structurally from an amine?
records.back: An amide N is bonded to C=O; an amine N is not.
accept: amide nitrogen is attached to a carbonyl carbon whereas an amine nitrogen is not
an amide has C(=O)-N bonding; an amine lacks that adjacent carbonyl
reject: an amine always has a carbonyl directly bonded to nitrogen
there is no structural difference between an amine and an amide

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: What type of mechanism is acyl chloride acylation?
records.back: Nucleophilic addition–elimination.
accept: nucleophilic addition followed by elimination
nucleophilic addition-elimination mechanism
reject: electrophilic substitution
free radical substitution

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: What makes the acyl carbon attractive to a nucleophile?
records.back: The carbonyl carbon is electron-poor (δ+).
accept: the partial positive carbonyl carbon is electrophilic
polar C=O leaves carbon electron deficient
reject: the carbonyl carbon has a full negative charge
nucleophiles attack because the acyl carbon has excess lone pairs

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: In acylation mechanisms, where should the nucleophile's arrow point?
records.back: Toward the electrophilic carbonyl carbon.
accept: curly arrow from nucleophile lone pair to carbonyl carbon
the arrow head points to the electron deficient carbon of C=O
reject: curly arrow begins at carbonyl carbon and ends at the nucleophile
arrow points towards the chloride rather than the carbonyl carbon during initial addition

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: What happens to the C=O bonding electron pair during initial attack?
records.back: It moves towards the oxygen atom.
accept: the carbonyl pi electrons move onto oxygen
a curly arrow goes from C=O pi bond to the oxygen atom
reject: the C=O electron pair moves onto chloride ion
the carbonyl pi electrons move to the nucleophile

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: What shape does the carbonyl carbon adopt in the addition intermediate?
records.back: Approximately tetrahedral.
accept: carbonyl carbon becomes roughly tetrahedral in the addition intermediate
the intermediate has tetrahedral arrangement at acyl carbon
reject: the carbonyl carbon stays linear during the nucleophilic addition
the intermediate carbonyl carbon has a 180 degree bond angle

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: What change reforms C=O during the elimination stage?
records.back: An oxygen lone pair reforms the carbon–oxygen double bond.
accept: oxygen lone pair returns to reform the carbonyl pi bond
the oxyanion lone pair forms C=O again
reject: chloride donates its lone pair to form the C=O bond
the carbonyl bond reforms by losing an electron from oxygen to solvent

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: Which type of species is displaced from an acyl chloride intermediate?
records.back: A chloride ion, Cl−, acts as the leaving group.
accept: chloride leaves as Cl-
a chloride ion is expelled from the tetrahedral intermediate
reject: an OH- ion leaves from the acyl chloride in this step
the acyl carbon atom is the leaving group

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: Why is nucleophilic acylation called addition–elimination?
records.back: The nucleophile adds before a leaving group is expelled.
accept: nucleophile addition is followed by leaving group elimination
an incoming nucleophile adds before chloride is expelled
reject: the leaving group is expelled before any nucleophile attacks
addition elimination means electrons are never transferred in bonds

records.subject: Maths
records.front: When does a geometric series have a sum to infinity, and what is it?
accept: for absolute r less than one the limiting sum is a divided by one minus r
|r|<1 and S_infinity=a/(1-r)
reject: a geometric series converges to a/(1-r) whenever r>1
the sum to infinity equals a/(1+r) for all ratios

records.subject: Maths
records.front: What does y=|f(x)| do to a graph?
records.back: Reflects any part below the x-axis in the x-axis; parts above stay unchanged.
accept: the negative portions of f(x) are reflected in the x-axis
parts with y below zero are mapped to positive y; positive parts stay put
reject: reflect the whole graph in the y-axis
the graph of |f(x)| retains negative y values

records.subject: Maths
records.front: What is the sum of the first n terms of an arithmetic sequence?
accept: half of n times first plus last term, S_n=n(a+l)/2

records.subject: Maths
records.front: What is the general term in (a+b)ⁿ?
records.back: C(n,r) a^(n−r) b^r.
accept: the general term is nCr multiplied by a to n-r multiplied by b to r
choose n r times a^(n-r) times b^r
reject: the general term is nCr a^r b^r
the general term is a^(n-r)+b^r

records.subject: Maths
records.front: What is the equation of a circle centre (a,b), radius r?
records.back: (x−a)²+(y−b)²=r².
accept: a circle centred at (a,b) has (x-a)^2+(y-b)^2=r^2
(x-a)^2+(y-b)^2 equals the radius squared
reject: (x+a)^2+(y+b)^2=r^2 for centre (a,b)

records.subject: Maths
records.front: How is a tangent to a circle related to the radius at the contact point?
records.back: They are perpendicular.
accept: radius and tangent are at right angles at their point of contact
the tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the touching point
reject: a tangent is parallel to the radius at contact
a circle tangent always passes through its centre

records.subject: Maths
records.front: What is the finite geometric sum?
records.back: Sₙ = a(1−rⁿ)/(1−r), for r≠1.
accept: sum equals a times (1-r to the n) divided by (1-r)
S_n=a(1-r^n)/(1-r), r not equal to one
reject: S_n=a/(1-r) for any finite n

records.subject: Maths
records.front: For positive integer n, what does x^(1/n) mean wherever it is real?
records.back: The real nth root of x.
accept: x^(1/n) is the nth root of x where real
raising x to one over n gives its real nth root
reject: x^(1/n) means x divided by n
x^(1/n) equals n times x

records.subject: Maths
records.front: For x ≠ 0 and positive integer n, what is x⁻ⁿ?
records.back: 1/xⁿ.
accept: x to negative n is the reciprocal of x to positive n
x^-n=1/(x^n) for nonzero x
reject: x^-n=-x^n
x^-n=x/n

records.subject: Maths
records.front: State the tan identity.
records.back: tan x = sin x / cos x.
accept: tan(x)=sin(x)/cos(x) wherever cos x is nonzero
the tangent ratio equals sine divided by cosine
reject: tan x=cos x/sin x
tan x=sin x times cos x

records.subject: Maths
records.front: What condition must a differentiable function satisfy at a stationary point?
accept: the first derivative must equal zero at a differentiable stationary point
stationary at x=a requires f'(a)=0
reject: a stationary point requires f(a)=0
a stationary point occurs whenever f''(a)=0

records.subject: Maths
records.front: What is a counterexample in mathematical proof?
records.back: One case showing a universal claim is false.
accept: a valid example that disproves a general assertion
one instance satisfying the assumptions where the claimed result fails
reject: an example which confirms the claim for one value
any value outside the specified domain

records.subject: Maths
records.front: What is the quadratic formula for ax² + bx + c = 0?
accept: x=(-b plus or minus sqrt(b^2-4ac))/(2a)
x equals minus b plus or minus the square root of discriminant all over 2a
reject: x=(b plus or minus sqrt(b^2-4ac))/(2a)
x=(-b plus or minus sqrt(b^2+4ac))/(2a)

records.subject: Maths
records.front: What is the sum of n terms of an arithmetic progression?
accept: the nth partial arithmetic sum is n/2[2a+(n-1)d]
S_n=n(a+l)/2 for first term a and last term l

records.subject: Maths
records.front: What is the sum of n terms of a geometric progression?
records.back: Sₙ = a(1−rⁿ)/(1−r), when r ≠ 1.
accept: for r not equal to one, S_n=a(1-r^n)/(1-r)
a times one minus r to n divided by one minus r
reject: S_n=a/(1-r) for every finite n
